In twenty twenty-three, the number of existing homes sold in America fell to its lowest level in almost thirty years.
After the two thousand eight crash, builders went bust or got very careful. For about a decade, America built far fewer homes than it needed.
Estimates of the shortage vary, from about one and a half million homes to several million. But nearly every expert agrees the country is short.
Zoning rules decide what can be built where. In many American cities, most of the land for homes is zoned only for single-family houses. No apartments. No duplexes.
And when builders do propose new homes, neighbors often show up to meetings to fight them. They worry about traffic, crowding, or their own home values.
Large investors own only a small share of single-family homes across the whole country. But in some fast-growing cities, like Atlanta, Phoenix and Charlotte, their share is much higher.

All of this has pushed first-time buyers later in life. In twenty twenty-five, the typical first-time buyer was forty years old, the oldest ever recorded.

Some cities have started changing their rules. Minneapolis ended single-family-only zoning in twenty eighteen. Austin cut its minimum lot size. Studies found rents in Minneapolis rose more slowly than in many similar cities.
